title: Apostrophes, quotation marks and end punctuation
blurb: Place apostrophes, quotation marks and end marks the American way, including the tricky question mark inside or outside a quotation.
question: A student writes, Did the nurse say, “Visiting hours end at eight”? Then she adds, The nurse said, “Please wait here”. One sentence follows US rules and one does not. Which, and why?

teach.body: Formally, an apostrophe marks a contraction or possession; quotation marks enclose a speaker's or writer's exact words and the titles of short works; end punctuation (period, question mark, exclamation point) closes a sentence according to its purpose. Plain English: US English has fixed placement rules here, and the TEAS tests them. The headline rule: periods and commas ALWAYS go inside the closing quotation mark.

teach.caption: Capitalize the first word of a quoted full sentence. A quotation inside a quotation uses single marks: “The sign says ‘Exit only,’ so go left.”
Rule of thumb: a part goes in quotation marks; the whole it belongs to goes in italics.

teach.note: An indirect question reports a question, so it ends with a period. Exclamation points are rare in formal writing.

teach.h: Scenario: Tyler writes a shift note
teach.body: Tyler Nguyen, a nursing applicant shadowing on a unit, records: The patient said, “I feel dizzy.” He places the period inside the closing mark (US rule) and capitalizes “I” because it begins a full quoted sentence. Later he summarizes: The patient asked whether she could stand. That is an indirect question, so no quotation marks, no comma after “asked,” and a period, not a question mark.

teach.text: The classic TEAS traps: a period or comma outside the closing quotation mark (British style), a question mark at the end of an indirect question, an apostrophe in a plain plural (RN's, 1990's), and “it's” used for “its.” Also watch for a semicolon placed inside the quotation marks: it belongs outside.

items: Apostrophes form contractions and possessives only, never plain plurals.
Periods and commas always go inside closing quotation marks; colons and semicolons outside.
A question mark goes inside if the quotation asks, outside if the whole sentence asks.
Direct quotes take quotation marks and a comma after the tag; indirect quotes take neither.
Short works in quotation marks, long works in italics; indirect questions end with a period.

summary: You can now use apostrophes only for contractions and possession, place every mark correctly around closing quotation marks in US style, and choose the right end punctuation for statements, commands and direct or indirect questions. You can also tell which titles take quotation marks and which take italics.

A.q: Which sentence follows US rules for punctuating a quotation?
options: The nurse said, “Please wait here”.
The nurse said “Please wait here.”
The nurse said, “Please wait here.”
The nurse said, “please wait here.”
A.why: A comma follows the dialogue tag, the quoted sentence is capitalized, and the period goes inside the closing mark.

whyNot.0: In US style, the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
whyNot.1: A comma is needed to separate the tag “said” from the quotation.
whyNot.3: The first word of a quoted full sentence must be capitalized.

A.q: Which sentence about the clinic is punctuated correctly?
options: She asked whether the clinic was open?
She asked whether the clinic was open.
She asked, “whether the clinic was open.”
She asked whether, the clinic was open.
A.why: This is an indirect question: it reports what she asked, so it ends with a period and uses no quotation marks.

whyNot.0: An indirect question is a statement about a question, so it ends with a period.
whyNot.2: Quotation marks are only for exact words; “whether the clinic was open” is reported speech.
whyNot.3: No comma belongs between “whether” and the rest of its clause.

options: In the 1990's, RNs said it's a long shift.
In the 1990s, RN's said it's a long shift.
In the 1990s, RNs said its a long shift.
In the 1990s, RNs said it's a long shift.
A.why: Plurals of numbers and capital abbreviations take no apostrophe (1990s, RNs), and it's means “it is.”

whyNot.0: 1990s is a plain plural, so it takes no apostrophe.
whyNot.1: RNs is a plain plural, so it takes no apostrophe.
whyNot.2: “It is a long shift” is meant, so the contraction it's needs its apostrophe.

B.q: Which sentence places the question mark correctly?
options: Did the doctor really say “no visitors”?
Did the doctor really say “no visitors?”
Did the doctor really say “no visitors.”?
Did the doctor really say, “no visitors”.
B.why: The whole sentence is the question; the quoted words are not. So the question mark goes outside.

whyNot.1: “No visitors” is not itself a question, so the question mark belongs outside.
whyNot.2: A sentence takes only one end mark; the period must go.
whyNot.3: The sentence is a question, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.

B.q: Which sentence about a patient's question is punctuated correctly?
options: The patient asked, “When can I go home”?
The patient asked, “When can I go home?”.
The patient asked “When can I go home?”
The patient asked, “When can I go home?”
B.why: The quoted words are the question, so the question mark goes inside, and nothing follows it.

whyNot.0: The quotation itself is the question, so its question mark goes inside.
whyNot.1: A sentence takes only one end mark; the extra period must go.
whyNot.2: A comma is needed after the dialogue tag “asked.”

B.q: Which sentence places the semicolon correctly?
options: The memo was titled “Shift Changes;” everyone read it.
The memo was titled “Shift Changes”; everyone read it.
The memo was titled “Shift Changes,” everyone read it.
The memo was titled “Shift Changes” everyone read it.
B.why: Semicolons always go outside closing quotation marks.

whyNot.0: A semicolon goes outside the closing quotation mark, not inside.
whyNot.2: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyNot.3: Two independent clauses with no punctuation make a run-on.

C.q: Rosa cites an article titled Sleep and Shift Work, published in a monthly magazine called Nursing Today. How should she format the two titles?
options: Italics for the article; quotation marks for the magazine
Quotation marks for both the article and the magazine
Quotation marks for the article; italics for the magazine
Italics for both the article and the magazine
C.why: An article is a short work (quotation marks); a magazine is a long work (italics).

whyNot.0: This reverses the rule: the short work gets quotation marks and the long work gets italics.
whyNot.1: A magazine is a long work, so it takes italics.
whyNot.3: An article is a short work, so it takes quotation marks.

C.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quotation within a quotation?
options: Ana said, “The sign says ‘Exit only,’ so use the side door.”
Ana said, “The sign says “Exit only,” so use the side door.”
Ana said, ‘The sign says “Exit only,” so use the side door.’
Ana said, “The sign says ‘Exit only’, so use the side door.”
C.why: US style uses double marks outside and single marks inside, with the comma inside the single mark.

whyNot.1: A quotation inside a quotation uses single marks, not a second set of doubles.
whyNot.2: Single marks outside and doubles inside is British style.
whyNot.3: The comma must go inside the closing single quotation mark.

C.q: A patient says, “I am dizzy.” Which sentence correctly reports this as an indirect quotation?
options: The patient said that “she was dizzy.”
The patient said that she was dizzy.
The patient said, that she was dizzy.
The patient said that, “she was dizzy.”
C.why: Indirect quotations report the meaning in the writer's words, with no quotation marks and no comma after “said.”

whyNot.0: “She was dizzy” are not the patient's exact words, so no quotation marks.
whyNot.2: No comma separates “said” from a “that” clause.
whyNot.3: This adds both a stray comma and quotation marks around words that were not spoken exactly.

reteach.title: Quotation marks are a fence
reteach.question: Think of quotation marks as a fence around someone's exact words. In the US, which pieces of punctuation live inside the fence, and which stay outside?

blocks.h: Small pets inside, big furniture outside
blocks.body: In US style, the little marks, periods and commas, always go inside the fence, even when they don't seem to belong to the quote. The bigger marks, colons and semicolons, always stay outside. Question marks and exclamation points are the visitors: they go inside only if they belong to the person speaking, and outside if they belong to the whole sentence.

blocks.text: British books put periods and commas outside the fence. The TEAS uses US rules, so “Wait here”. is wrong and “Wait here.” is right.

explain.body: Use an apostrophe for missing letters (they're = they are) or possession (nurses' station). Plain plurals and possessive pronouns never take one.

test.q: Which sentence about the nurses uses apostrophes correctly?
options: The nurse's are sure they're ready.
The nurses are sure their ready.
The nurses' are sure they're ready.
The nurses are sure they're ready.
test.why: Nurses is a plain plural (no apostrophe), and they're means “they are.”

whyNot.0: Nurses is a plain plural here, so it takes no apostrophe.
whyNot.1: “They are ready” is meant, so the contraction they're is needed.
whyNot.2: Nothing belongs to the nurses, so no possessive apostrophe.

explain.body: In US style, periods and commas always go inside closing quotation marks. Colons and semicolons always go outside.

test.q: Which sentence quoting a medication label is punctuated correctly?
options: “Take one tablet daily,” the label says.
“Take one tablet daily”, the label says.
“Take one tablet daily.” the label says.
“Take one tablet daily” the label says.
test.why: A comma ends the quoted sentence when a tag follows, and in US style it goes inside the closing mark.

whyNot.1: In US style the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
whyNot.2: When the sentence continues with a tag, the quote ends with a comma, not a period.
whyNot.3: A comma is needed to separate the quotation from the tag.

explain.body: Ask who is asking. If the quoted words are a question, the mark goes inside. If the whole sentence is the question, it goes outside, and the quote's own period disappears.

test.q: Which question about the lab places its question mark correctly?
options: Who said, “The lab is closed?”
Who said, “The lab is closed.”?
Who said, “The lab is closed”?
Who said “The lab is closed?”.
test.why: The whole sentence asks the question, and the quoted words are a statement, so the question mark goes outside.

whyNot.0: The quoted words are a statement, not a question, so the mark goes outside.
whyNot.1: A sentence takes only one end mark; the quote's period is dropped.
whyNot.3: The question mark is on the wrong side and an extra period is added.

explain.body: Statements, commands and indirect questions end with a period. Direct questions end with a question mark. Exclamation points show strong feeling and are rare in formal writing.

test.q: Which of these sentences, shown without its end mark, should end with a question mark?
options: She wondered whether the clinic was still open
Can you tell me whether the clinic is open
Please tell me whether the clinic is open
I asked whether the clinic was open
test.why: “Can you tell me...” directly asks the reader something, so it is a direct question.

whyNot.0: This reports what she wondered: an indirect question, ending with a period.
whyNot.2: This is a polite command, which ends with a period.
whyNot.3: This reports a question that was asked: an indirect question, ending with a period.
